subsections.subsection_title: 48. COUNSELLING SCENARIO — “WILL MY BABY BE OKAY?”

blocks.text: “Most babies delivered with forceps do well, but there are some risks including bruising or temporary facial marks, and less commonly facial nerve injury or other trauma. The neonatal team will assess your baby after birth, particularly because we are using an assisted delivery.”

content_groups.group_title: Q1. What are the indications for forceps?

blocks.text: Fetal compromise requiring expedited birth, maternal indications such as exhaustion or ineffective pushing, and prolonged or arrested second stage where vaginal delivery remains appropriate.

Full cervical dilatation, ruptured membranes, engaged fetal head, known fetal position, appropriate station, no significant suspicion of cephalopelvic disproportion, adequate analgesia, empty bladder, informed consent where possible, skilled operator and appropriate backup.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. Why must the fetal position be known?

blocks.text: Because the blades must be correctly positioned around the fetal head and the direction of traction depends on the fetal head position.

content_groups.group_title: Q4. What happens if the forceps don't lock easily?

blocks.text: I would not force them. I would stop and reassess the fetal head position and blade placement.

content_groups.group_title: Q5. What are the major maternal complications?

blocks.text: Vaginal and perineal trauma, third- and fourth-degree tears, postpartum haemorrhage and, in the longer term, urinary or faecal incontinence and pelvic-floor dysfunction.

content_groups.group_title: Q6. What are the major neonatal complications?

blocks.text: Facial bruising and trauma, facial nerve palsy, cephalohaematoma and, rarely, skull or intracranial injury.

content_groups.group_title: Q7. Which has a higher risk of severe perineal trauma: vacuum or forceps?

blocks.text: Forceps generally carry a higher risk of maternal perineal trauma, including severe perineal tears.

content_groups.group_title: Q8. Which has a higher risk of scalp trauma?

“I would first confirm the indication for operative vaginal delivery and assess the maternal and fetal condition. I would obtain informed consent where circumstances permit and explain the procedure, benefits, risks and alternatives, including the possibility of Caesarean delivery if the procedure fails. I would ensure appropriate analgesia, empty the bladder and confirm full cervical dilatation, ruptured membranes, cephalic presentation, an engaged head, known fetal position, appropriate station and no significant suspicion of cephalopelvic disproportion. I would perform a careful vaginal examination to identify the fetal position and then select and apply the appropriate forceps blades carefully around the fetal head, ensuring that maternal tissue is not trapped. After confirming correct application, I would lock the blades and apply controlled traction along the pelvic axis during contractions and maternal pushing, reassessing descent after each traction. If there is no descent, fetal deterioration or any concern regarding safety, I would stop, seek senior assistance and reassess the mode of delivery. Following birth, I would assess the mother for genital tract trauma and haemorrhage and the baby for facial and other injuries.”
